extracted.intended_audience: fans of stand-up comedy, comedy historians, and practicing stand-up performers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and implicit criteria for preparing and presenting stand-up comedy on network late-night television (what to perform, how to present it, and what to expect from producers and censors). Useful for comedians planning short TV appearances and writers analyzing censorship/risk on broadcast TV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize strongest material for limited TV time
rubrics_metrics.description: When allotted only a short segment on a late-night show, use your strongest material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes Bill Hicks 'felt constrained by the limited amount of time he had to work with in his appearances... but he typically used his strongest material for these segments.' Implies bits should be concise, high-impact, and chosen to maximize effect in a brief slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress and presentation should match tone/mood
rubrics_metrics.description: Wardrobe and visible presentation matter for TV appearances and can reflect the mood you want to project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bill Hicks deliberately chose 'bright fall colors—an outfit bought just for the show and reflective of my bright and cheerful mood.' Presentation choices can influence audience perception and possibly network reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect producer and network Standards & Practices oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Segments are subject to producer approval and network Standards & Practices review and can be cut even after producer sign-off.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hicks's routine was 'approved and re-approved' by the segment producer but was later cut by CBS Standards and Practices. The account stresses that approval by producers does not guarantee airing; anticipate last-minute removals and fight/appeals may not succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid or mitigate 'hot button' controversial topics on broadcast TV
rubrics_metrics.description: References to highly sensitive topics (e.g., religion, the pro‑life movement, partisan politics) increase risk of censorship on network television.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece says Hicks’s routine 'with its references to Christians and the pro-life movement, hit too many hot buttons for David Letterman to allow it on the air.' For network late-night, controversial subject matter may be disallowed or require rewording.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor content for broad audience appeal and affiliate sensitivities
rubrics_metrics.description: Hosts and networks often modify show tone and material to broaden appeal and placate affiliates; performers should choose material that aligns with that strategy if they want to be aired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Letterman 'changed how he approached the show in order to broaden his appeal'—wearing tailored suits and monitoring content more closely. The article contrasts Letterman's approach with Jay Leno's focus on 'wider appeal' and studying ratings to suit popular tastes. This implies selecting material that won't alienate mass audiences or affiliates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that ratings and host/network strategy shape content decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Programming choices are influenced by ratings competition and the host/network's strategic decisions; material that jeopardizes ratings or affiliate relationships may be suppressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests Letterman aired Hicks’s routine in 2009 partly because he had 'given up in the ratings war' and later felt freer to revisit censorship decisions. Networks/hosts optimize for ratings and may avoid material perceived as risky for audience size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and timing affect whether contentious material can be aired
rubrics_metrics.description: A routine deemed unacceptable at one time may be acceptable later due to changed circumstances (host stance, ratings pressure, public opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dave later aired Hicks’s censored routine in 2009 and publicly admitted the earlier cut was his decision. The article notes Letterman's increased willingness to tangle with political figures in later years, suggesting that timing, host evolution, and cultural shifts can alter censorship outcomes.
